Although Google stopped making their version, similar devices are still being developed. Smartwatches are very popular and can do many things a smartphone can, like making calls, showing messages, tracking fitness, and even working independently if they have their own SIM card. Smart jewelry combines fashion with technology, offering features like changing LED colors to show notifications or tracking sun exposure to protect your skin. Smart footwear includes shoes that generate power from your steps to run sensors, insoles that track your walking patterns and health, and socks with sensors that help athletes improve their running technique.

In fitness and health, devices like Fitbit or Jawbone track your heart rate, calories burned, and activity levels. Some combine style and function, like solar-powered fitness trackers. There are also specialized devices like FitGuard, a mouth-guard for athletes that detects impacts and warns coaches about possible injuries. Golfers can use devices like the M-Tracer, which attaches to a club and records swing data to help improve their game.

Biomedical applications of HCI include smart contact lenses that can measure glucose levels in tears for people with diabetes. Bionic contact lenses can display information directly on the lens using harvested energy. New fingerprint scanners use ultrasound to read prints through phone covers and even through sweat or lotion, improving security. Bio-stamps are flexible sensors that stick to the skin like temporary tattoos and monitor things like temperature and blood pressure without bulky equipment. Closed-loop insulin delivery systems automatically monitor blood sugar and deliver insulin as needed, reducing the need for manual injections. Brain-controlled robotics allow people with paralysis or amputations to control prosthetic limbs or robotic arms using their thoughts.

In the automotive world, cars are becoming smarter with features like automatic lane changes and cruise control that keeps a safe distance from other vehicles. Tesla’s Autopilot can drive the car itself and alert the driver in emergencies. Heads-up displays project important information onto the windshield, so drivers don’t have to look away from the road. Some apps can turn your smartphone into a projection device for navigation. Safety gear for motor racing includes suits with sensors that detect crashes and deploy airbags instantly. There are also car seats equipped with sensors to detect if a driver is having a heart attack and can take control of the vehicle to stop safely. Apps exist to monitor driving habits and provide feedback to help drivers improve and even get insurance discounts.

Smart home technology focuses on saving energy and making life easier. Smart thermostats like Nest learn your schedule and adjust heating automatically, while others let you control temperature remotely. Smart LED bulbs can detect when a room is empty and turn off or adjust lighting to mimic natural daylight, which can also improve home security by simulating occupancy when you’re away.

Other emerging technologies include personal assistants like Siri and Google Now, which respond to voice commands to perform tasks like sending messages or checking the weather. Baby monitors now can track a baby’s heart rate, oxygen levels, and movement, sending real-time updates to parents’ phones. Real-time language translation tools on smartphones help break down language barriers by translating speech or text instantly. There are even devices like the Pavlok wristband that help people break bad habits by giving a mild electric shock as a reminder.

Overall, HCI is making technology more natural and integrated into our lives. We can expect future research to focus on improving real-time language translation, better eye and gesture tracking, more accurate biometric authentication, and more advanced augmented reality applications. As these technologies develop, they will continue to change how we interact with computers and the world around us.
